pages.x: Philip II of Spain, the most powerful king in Europe, was a devout Catholic. Protestant England under Elizabeth I helped the Dutch rebels fighting Spain, and English privateers raided Spanish treasure ships. When Elizabeth executed the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1587, Philip decided to invade.

In 1587 Drake sailed into Cádiz harbour and burned some 30 of the ships being made ready, which he called singeing the king of Spain's beard. It held the Armada back a year. The tale that he finished his game of bowls when it was sighted is a legend.

In May 1588 some 130 ships with nearly 30,000 men left Lisbon under the Duke of Medina Sidonia, who had little experience at sea. They were to sail up the Channel, meet the Duke of Parma's army in Flanders and carry it across to England.

English ships harried the Armada up the Channel, but its tight crescent held. Then, at anchor off Calais on the night of 7 August, it was attacked by eight burning ships sent in on the tide. The Spanish cut their cables and scattered, and the next day were beaten at Gravelines.

At Tilbury, Elizabeth rode among her soldiers waiting for the invasion and told them she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, but the heart and stomach of a king. By then the danger had already passed.

With the wind against them, the Spanish sailed home the long way, round Scotland and Ireland, into terrible storms. Perhaps a third of the ships were lost, and many men drowned or were killed on the Irish coast.
pages.of: of the Armada's men never came home

pages.x: English medals for the victory read: God blew, and they were scattered. Philip is said to have answered that he had sent his ships to fight men, not the winds.

The defeat saved Protestant England and the Dutch revolt and became a national legend. But the war went on for 16 more years, Spain rebuilt its fleet, and England's own armada of 1589 failed too. Its rise as a sea power had only begun.
